title: Considering Calendar-Aging High-Precision State of Health Estimation and Active Management Technology for Energy-Storage Batteries
abstract: As a core component of the new power system, energy-storage batteries undergo capacity degradation, increasing internal resistance and declining state of health (SOH) as a result of calendar aging. These changes compromise the operational safety and life-cycle economic performance of energy-storage stations. To address the need for calendar-aging risk management in stationary batteries and accurate SOH estimation from cycling data, this study develops two complementary components: a field priority-charging strategy for stationary cells and a data-driven SOH prediction model evaluated on public cycling datasets. The strategy defines criteria for low-energy stationary batteries and establishes weighted priority-charging rules for risk-cell locking and power replenishment. We construct an SOH prediction model that integrates interactive convolution and adaptive spectral modules, and we use the Dream Optimization Algorithm to optimize its hyperparameters and address multi-scale feature entanglement and limited prediction accuracy. The results show that the strategy replenishes SOC and increases cell voltage in stationary batteries, and that the risk score is significantly correlated with SOH. On the CALCE and Oxford cycling datasets, the model yields lower errors than the evaluated baselines, although the reduction depends on the battery and comparator. Ablation tests confirm the superiority of each module. This study provides a field risk-management scheme for stationary batteries and a high-precision SOH prediction method validated on public cycling datasets.
title_zh: Considering Calendar-Aging High-Precision State of Health Estimation and Active Management Technology for Energy-Storage Batteries

title: Vehicle Type Heterogeneity in Battery Electric Vehicle Energy Consumption: A Multi-Perspective Analysis Using Real-World Fleet Data
abstract: Real-world energy consumption of battery electric vehicles (BEVs) varies with trip conditions, driving behavior, and vehicle state. Treating vehicle type merely as a control variable may mask substantial heterogeneity in energy consumption mechanisms. This study treats vehicle type as a source of mechanism heterogeneity and examines how the determinants of energy consumption rate (ECR) differ among sedans, logistics vehicles, and buses. Using 41,933 trips in China, we combined statistical analysis, machine learning, and CausalForestDML. Statistically, ECRs of sedans and logistics vehicles decrease as trip distance increases, but trip distance is nearly irrelevant for buses. Aggressive driving raises logistics vehicle ECR by 22.2% yet barely affects sedans. For prediction, permutation importance further reveals the divergence: trip distance and duration dominate sedan prediction, whereas energy recovery ratio and accelerator-pedal, which are marginally important for sedans, become primary predictors for logistics vehicles and buses. Causal estimates confirm that directional divergences persist after conditioning on covariates. For example, trip duration has opposite effects on buses versus sedans and logistics vehicles. Moreover, the causal framework decomposes each factor’s effects across its value range, revealing patterns beyond correlation alone. These findings provide actionable guidance for vehicle-specific eco-driving strategies and battery management system optimization.
title_zh: Vehicle Type Heterogeneity in Battery Electric Vehicle Energy Consumption: A Multi-Perspective Analysis Using Real-World Fleet Data
